newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Two Brazil coffee exporting groups may unite.
newsitem.headline: Two Brazil coffee exporting groups may unite.

text.p: Brazil's coffee exporting community, for 1-1/2 years divided into two groups, may be on the road to uniting, officials said.

A meeting of officials from the Brazilian Coffee Exporters Federations (FEBEC) in Vitoria today decided to hold talks with the Brazilian Coffee Exporters Association (Abecafe) to see if there is a way to bring the two groups together.
"We are going to have a meeting with Abecafe to see the possibility of having a new institution together," said FEBEC president Oswaldo Aranha.
"I am happy. This is the first step towards a union," said Abecafe president Jorge Esteve on hearing the news.
FEBEC is the traditional exporters' group but in November 1995 a group of exporters formed Abecafe, principally because they opposed a private sector plan dividing out coffee exports internally.
The association has gradually grown in size and now has 45 members, accounting for around 47 percent of Brazilian coffee exports in 1996, according to Abecafe statistics.
One of the main points of division last year was the creation of Brazil's new coffee council, called the CDPC, which united the private coffee sector and government officials.
However only place was alloted to the exporting sector, with FEBEC officially chosen as the representative exporters' body which resulted in a wave of protests from Abecafe.
With elections for all FEBEC officers due to be held at the end of this month however, market talk about attempts to reconcile the two groups started to surface over the past month.
The negotiation process is likely however to take longer than a few weeks and Febec elections may need to be delayed.
Traders expect to see changes in FEBEC's by-laws - and even a new name.
"We have to start from scratch. It is like a merger," Aranha said after the meeting.

Abecafe members were already planning to hold their annual general assembly on April 15 in Santos and now there will be a special session that same day to discuss what members want from a possible new institution, Esteve said.
Then it is likely a commission will be set up with three members each from Abecafe and Febec to discuss how the two groups could come together.

The issue of open or regulated market is unlikely to cause any problems at the current time despite imminent talks by members of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) on market stabilisation plans from July 1997.

Brazil has found it painless to work under the current ACPC export quota of 15 million bags during 1996/97, and with the prospect of a smaller crop in 1997/98, it should not have to restrict exports in order to fulfill any shipment allocation expected at least to equal, if not exceed, 1996/97.
Also, some traders said, Abecafe's own attitude to market intervention has changed slightly in that it accepts minimal participation by governments in the market.
This, they say, is demonstrated by its view the Brazilian government should maintain a working stock of between five and seven million bags to allow for times of crisis such as frost.
Given that the government currently is holding around 12 million bags of stocks, it will be some years before it will need to actually buy fresh reserves.
But Abecafe feels it is important to plan ahead so that when the time comes, there will be sufficient funds to enter the market, traders said.
((-Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151))
